Dancing for Your Life

By: Sinethemba Nogude | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
What if you literally had to dance for survival? We all have seen those groups of kids who enthusiastically perform for you whilst you are in traffic… we may clap at the talent they have or offer lo

Unique Selling Point:
South Africa is more famous than any other nation in the world for its distinctive dance
moves and development of creative dance movements. From the famous Pantsula dancers
who have graced world stages, to what some of you would know the famous Gwara-Gwara
dance Beyonce took a liking to. Bottom line is that we have the best dancers in the world…
But guys… What if you literally had to dance for survival? We all have seen those groups of
kids who enthusiastically perform for you whilst you are in traffic… we may clap at the talent
they have or offer loose change as a gesture of appreciation, but do we ever wonder about
them? What their story is? I had the privilege of spending weeks with these kids… mainly
from Alex. You may be frustrated with them, but after watching the story, your perspective
about them will change just as mine changed when I went into their homes and spent time
with them.
Alexandra
These youngsters come from Alexandra township which is one of the poorest areas in the
country and is located next to the wealthy suburb of Sandton. Alexandra has huge rates of
unemployment, over-population and a high crime rate. Even though I was with them, I was
scared to take out my phone from my pocket. I learned that these they live with their
mothers, absent fathers and depend solely on SASSA grant money are very poor but their
courage to do what they do will open doors for them.
Characters
There are about 6 or 7 of them in the crew, but I chose three characters who will drive the
story, they speak well, they’re passionate and they have strong background stories.
Sanele Mncwabe, 28-year-old who stays with his parents. Sanele had a business that kept
him busy, but things didn’t work out and so he decided to start a dancing group in order to
stay away from crime. He’s their leader of this group and he comes up with dance moves
and routines
Kwanele Zikode, 17 years old of age, does grade 9 at Alex High. He stays with his mother and
his twin sister. Their father died when he was in Creche. His mother works at the
Municipality. He started dancing in 2019 and believes that it’s not all about money but for
exposure. Becoming a dancer one day is what keeps him awake at night, “I sometimes get
home at 8pm and just think about becoming a professional dancer.”
Sthembiso Buthelezi, 18, and he’s in grade 10. He stays with his mother who’s a tailor,
Sthembiso uses his talent of dancing to contribute at home “Just like a man should do when
staying with a single mother.” Dancing also helps him to stay out of trouble.
How the story will be told
I think this piece would need to be quite cinematic and beautiful – meeting the kids at
home early in the morning, filming them changing into their costumes and taking the
trip into the suburbs with them. Going home with them to see what they do with their
evening after the dancing is done. A “day in the life” approach. There will be lot of close
ups and slow motions of the dancing.

Security for two shooting days

Script: Dancing for your life

Opening Sequence: Slow-mo visuals of Siyathemba dancing with intensity

Upsound Siyathemba: When I dance, everything disappears
Transition into the next shots of Kwanele dancing with intensity.
Upsound Kwanele: Dancing is an escape for me..
Transition into the next shots of Francisco dancing.
Upsound Franscisco: I am dancing for my life.
[Dip to black]

V/O For these young men, dancing is survival... their stage: the busy Joburg intersections where they spend weekends... hoping for spare change from passing motorists.
But have you ever wondered who they are … and how they got here?

SEGUE TO DRONE ESTABLISHING SEQUENCE [GVs of Alex into sequence of Siyathemba waking up and getting ready]

V/O: Alexandra township is one of the oldest in the country and Gauteng’s most violent and impoverished - here they call it “Gomora.
Siyathemba Mbatha wakes up every Saturday to get ready for his eight-hour shift at the city's busiest intersections - “clocking in” means putting on his dancing shoes.

Upsound 00:02:27 Xola: What is it about dance that you like?

Upsound Siyethemba: 00:25:51 Dance is what I love. I started dancing in 2008What I like is that it inspires young people, they look towards us, and we inspire them.

V/O: Like many young people here, Siyathemba quit school to look for work and help support his family.

Upsound: 00:14:57 Siyethemba: Life here in Gomora is very tough for most of us and there aren't much opportunities, so you have to go out of our hood…to make a living.
V/O: Facing a staggering unemployment rate, where two out of three young people won’t find jobs, Siyathemba turned to dance and looked for others in Alex wanting to be part of his eight-member crew.
Upsound 00:09:22 Siyethemba: I told the young boys that there's a way of entertainment, luckily some of them liked dancing, so I pulled them all in and we started making money. [breather]
V/O: One of the first to join was 17-year-old Kwanele Zikode who dreams of being a professional dancer.
Upsound 00:01:04Kwanele: I love dancing , I told him that I'm interested. We started rehearsing, after 10 days we then we went to Rosebank
00:05:25 Thandiwe: I can't stop him because it's something that he loved from an early age. [drone shot into Walking sequence Lihle Nene]
V/O: Dancing is Kwanele’s refuge.
Upsound 00:00:52 Kwanele: You sleep hearing gunshots and wake up hearing gunshots. We are even scared of walking in the street, That's why Siyathemba has put us in Pantsula.
V/O: For Kwanele's mother Thandiwe Zikode, everyday’s uncertain.
00:07:08 Thandiwe I’m always worried because I don't know what is happening, it's in the street and I'm always thankful when I see him coming back alive.
Upsound Xola 00:22 How difficult is it for these boys to break out of the situation.
Upsoud Lihle 0:52 Talking about arts, it needs space They need a conducive space so that they can practice but there's less of those spaces here you know so the only space we have is just if field and the space is a street.
V/O: At a high school in Alex, art teacher Lihle Nene has some of these dancers in his class and despite the risks, he encourages this creative outlet.
Upsound Lihle 04:00 So it's a serious challenge for these guys. And when you go to the robots, you see them dancing, and others are looking at them a bit with a... It's a bit appalling for them,they don't even consider the amount of focus they invest in mastering those sequences.
[breather]
V/O: It’s payday weekend and it should be the crew's most profitable time. Before heading to the city, they rehearse for a few hours.
Link Xola in alley: what for me might seem like a little adventure, a little excitement and maybe a little dangerous is nothing more than daily life for Siyathemba and his crew, as they make their way to practice this way every single day.
[Walking through shacks sequence]
Upsound Xola 0:03 Are you strict with the boys ?
Upsound Siyathemba 0:05 I am very strict
Upsound Siyathemba 0:19 We do need discipline for us to move forward.
Upsound Xola : So this is where you practice?
Upsound Siyathemba: yes.
V/O: Without proper recreational facilities in Alex, they use an abandoned factory to practice.
Upsound dancing session: [Siyathemba giving out instruction, intense dancing]
V/O: Siyathemba pushes them hard - but 15 year old Francisco Dlamini doesn’t mind. Like the others he’s hoping dance will give him a way out.
Upsound Franscisco 02:20 I was inspired by Siyathemba. We don’t only go there to just dance, we are hoping to get sponsors so that we can travel to other countries.
V/O: After rehearsal - it’s time to work. They all chip in for the taxi fare to Rosebank.
[Visuals of Xola and the boys in the taxi]
V/O: It's only 15 kilometres away, but it feels like a world apart from the grind of their daily lives. Their excitement is palpable.
Upsound Xola in Car and crew in Taxi
V/O: They set up at their usual intersection.
Sequence of crew dancing and collecting money in traffic.
V/O: But after only 30 minutes, they’re forced to stop. [build tension with visuals of the crew just sitting around]
Link: Then loadshedding happens , so what now?
V/O: With traffic lights out, they decide against taking chances.
Upsound Kwanene 00:05:32Kwanele: There's another boy who got hit by a car, he's still alive And another one got hit by a car and he didn't survive..
[Siyathemba interview at intersection]
Upsound Xola 0:55 So Syathemba what is happening now?
Upsound Siyathemba 01:03 We usually change intersections and go to Mcdonalds…Guys let's get to it.
V/O: They relocate to a part of Rosebank on a different load-shedding schedule. It’s a frustrating start. [Drone visual of in intersection]
[Dancing upsound]
[Visuals of Xola trying]
[breather..dancing]
V/O: It’s been a tough day - netting only a few hundred rand. But they remain upbeat.
Upsound 00:13:54 Xola: How far do you think this thing can go?
Upsound 00:13:56 Siyethemba: I think this thing can go too far only if we can be serious about it and use money wisely because we do want to make dance a career.
V/O: For now, though, this is their reality; their dreams dependent on the generosity of strangers.
[end]

I learned that these they live with their mothers, absent fathers and depend solely on SASSA grant money are very poor but their courage to do what they do will open doors for them. Characters There are about 6 or 7 of them in the crew, but I chose three characters who will drive the story, they speak well, they’re passionate and they have strong background stories. Sanele Mncwabe, 28-year-old who stays with his parents. Sanele had a business that kept him busy, but things didn’t work out and so he decided to start a dancing group in order to stay away from crime. He’s their leader of this group and he comes up with dance moves and routines Kwanele Zikode, 17 years old of age, does grade 9 at Alex High. He stays with his mother and his twin sister. Their father died when he was in Creche. His mother works at the Municipality. He started dancing in 2019 and believes that it’s not all about money but for exposure. Becoming a dancer one day is what keeps him awake at night, “I sometimes get home at 8pm and just think about becoming a professional dancer.” Sthembiso Buthelezi, 18, and he’s in grade 10. He stays with his mother who’s a tailor, Sthembiso uses his talent of dancing to contribute at home “Just like a man should do when staying with a single mother.” Dancing also helps him to stay out of trouble. How the story will be told I think this piece would need to be quite cinematic and beautiful – meeting the kids at home early in the morning, filming them changing into their costumes and taking the trip into the suburbs with them. Going home with them to see what they do with their evening after the dancing is done. A “day in the life” approach. There will be lot of close ups and slow motions of the dancing.
